items.message:
📌 10 Ghi Chú Cốt Tủy: Thái Cực Quyền, Khí Công & Cơ Sinh Học Cân Mạc (Taichi-ChiGong)

Ghi Chú 01: Khái Niệm "Tùng" (Sung) — Khử Co Cứng Đối Kháng

Bản chất: Tùng không phải là buông xuôi nhẽo cơ mà là trạng thái giải tỏa co thắt cơ vân đối kháng (antagonist muscle inhibition), cho phép năng lượng truyền tải tự do qua các khớp.

Cơ chế cân mạc: Giảm ma sát nội mô, tăng dịch bôi trơn hyaluronic acid giữa các lớp màng cân mạc (fascial glide).

Ứng dụng thực hành: Khi đứng Trạm Trang, liên tục rà soát quét từ đỉnh đầu xuống bàn chân để "tháo van" mọi điểm gồng cứng vô thức.

Ghi Chú 02: Hư Linh Đỉnh Kình & Trục Cột Sống Treo

🔗 https://taichinow.github.io/articles/01_taichi_qigong_10_notes

#ThaiCucQuyen #TaichiNow #SucKhoe

— Phạm Đức Hải

📌 10 Ghi Chú Cốt Tủy: Y Học Cổ Truyền (TCM), Kinh Lạc & Năng Lượng Tự Chữa Lành

Ghi Chú 01: Đồng Hồ Sinh Học 12 Kinh Lạc (TCM Circadian Organ Clock)

Bản chất: Mỗi tạng phủ có 2 giờ hoạt động với năng lượng khí huyết cao nhất trong ngày.

Quy luật: Phế (3-5h), Đại Trường (5-7h), Vị (7-9h), Tỳ (9-11h), Tâm (11-13h), Tiểu Trường (13-15h), Bàng Quang (15-17h), Thận (17-19h), Tâm Bào (19-21h), Tam Tiêu (21-23h), Đởm (23-1h), Can (1-3h).

Ứng dụng: Không ăn đêm sau 20h để tránh cản trở Can-Đởm giải độc và phục hồi tủy.

Ghi Chú 02: Trục Thận Thủy - Tâm Hỏa (Thủy Hỏa Ký Tế)

Bản chất: Thận thủy cần bốc lên làm mát Tâm hỏa; Tâm hỏa cần giáng xuống sưởi ấm Thận thủy.

🔗 https://taichinow.github.io/articles/02_health_tcm_energy_10_notes

#ThaiCucQuyen #TaichiNow #SucKhoe

— Phạm Đức Hải

items.message:
📌 10 Ghi Chú Cốt Tủy: Tuổi 52 — Hành Trình Tu Tập Nội Tại & Trí Tuệ Sống

Ghi Chú 01: Quy Luật "Ngũ Thập Tri Thiên Mệnh"

Ý nghĩa cốt lõi: Tuổi 50 không phải là sự già nua, mà là điểm khởi đầu của trí tuệ chín muồi. Biết rõ giới hạn của bản thân và hiểu quy luật của vũ trụ để sống thuận tự nhiên.

Tâm thế sống: Chuyển từ "chinh phục thế giới bên ngoài" sang "làm chủ thế giới nội tâm".

Ứng dụng: Buông bỏ nhu cầu chứng tỏ bản thân với xã hội, chỉ giữ lại những kết nối chân thành.

Ghi Chú 02: Tái Cấu Trúc Trục Cơ Thể Sau Tuổi 50

Thực trạng: Các đĩa đệm cột sống mất nước, mật độ xương giảm, các khớp gối và háng dễ thoái hóa nếu vận động sai trục.

🔗 https://taichinow.github.io/articles/03_tuoi_52_tu_tap_noi_tai_10_notes

#ThaiCucQuyen #TaichiNow #SucKhoe

— Phạm Đức Hải

items.message:
📌 10 Ghi Chú Cốt Tủy: Chủ Nghĩa Thiết Yếu & Tối Giản Tài Chính (Minimalism & Essentialism)

Ghi Chú 01: Quy Luật "Ít Hơn Nhưng Tốt Hơn" (Less But Better - Weniger aber besser)

Bản chất: Cốt lõi của chủ nghĩa thiết yếu không phải là cắt giảm cực đoan, mà là tối ưu hóa chất lượng trong từng lựa chọn.

Tác động tài chính: Loại bỏ 80% các khoản chi tiêu vô thưởng vô phạt để dồn 100% nguồn lực vào những trải nghiệm và tài sản sinh lời thực sự.

Ứng dụng: Trước mỗi quyết định mua sắm, tự hỏi: "Món đồ này có thực sự phục vụ cho mục tiêu cốt lõi của đời mình không?".

Ghi Chú 02: Quy Tắc 90% Trong Đánh Giá Quyết Định

🔗 https://taichinow.github.io/articles/04_minimalism_essentialism_10_notes

#ThaiCucQuyen #TaichiNow #SucKhoe

— Phạm Đức Hải

items.message:
📌 10 Ghi Chú Cốt Tủy: Tự Lực & Trí Tuệ Thực Hành Đời Sống (Self-Help & Practical Wisdom)

Ghi Chú 01: Sức Mạnh Của Những Thói Quen Nguyên Tử (Atomic Habits)

Quy luật tích lũy: Tiến bộ 1% mỗi ngày tương đương với việc bạn sẽ giỏi hơn gấp 37 lần sau một năm.

Công thức 4 bước: Gợi ý (Cue) ──► Khao khát (Craving) ──► Phản hồi (Response) ──► Phần thưởng (Reward).

Ứng dụng: Ghép thói quen mới vào sau một thói quen cũ đã có sẵn (Habit Stacking).

Ghi Chú 02: Trọng Tâm Vào Hệ Thống Thay Vì Mục Tiêu (Systems over Goals)

Bản chất: Mục tiêu chỉ cho bạn biết hướng đi; hệ thống và quy trình thực hiện hàng ngày mới là thứ mang lại kết quả.

🔗 https://taichinow.github.io/articles/05_self_help_practical_wisdom_10_notes

#ThaiCucQuyen #TaichiNow #SucKhoe

— Phạm Đức Hải

items.message:
📌 10 Ghi Chú Cốt Tủy: Huấn Luyện & Luyện Tập Có Chủ Đích (Coaching & Deliberate Practice)

Ghi Chú 01: Sự Khác Biệt Giữa Luyện Tập Thường (Naive Practice) & Có Chủ Đích (Deliberate Practice)

Luyện tập thường: Lặp đi lặp lại một hành động quen thuộc một cách vô thức, không có phản hồi và không có thử thách.

Luyện tập có chủ đích (Anders Ericsson): Mục tiêu cụ thể, tập trung 100%, vượt ra ngoài vùng thoải mái, có phản hồi tức thì và hiệu chỉnh liên tục.

Ứng dụng: Mỗi buổi tập Thái Cực hay kỹ năng đều phải có 1 mục tiêu kỹ thuật cụ thể cần cải thiện (ví dụ: chỉ tập trung mở khớp háng Kua trong 30 phút).

Ghi Chú 02: Xây Dựng Biểu Tượng Tinh Thần Đỉnh Cao (Mental Representations)

🔗 https://taichinow.github.io/articles/06_coaching_deliberate_practice_10_notes

#ThaiCucQuyen #TaichiNow #SucKhoe

— Phạm Đức Hải

Luyện tập thường: Lặp đi lặp lại một hành động quen thuộc một cách vô thức, không có phản hồi và không có thử thách.

Luyện tập có chủ đích (Anders Ericsson): Mục tiêu cụ thể, tập trung 100%, vượt ra ngoài vùng thoải mái, có phản hồi tức thì và hiệu chỉnh liên tục.

Ứng dụng: Mỗi buổi tập Thái Cực hay kỹ năng đều phải có 1 mục tiêu kỹ thuật cụ thể cần cải thiện (ví dụ: chỉ tập trung mở khớp háng Kua trong 30 phút).

Ghi Chú 02: Xây Dựng Biểu Tượng Tinh Thần Đỉnh Cao (Mental Representations)

items.message:
📌 10 Ghi Chú Cốt Tủy: Tâm Lý Học Hành Vi & Triết Học Đời Sống (Psychology & Philosophy)

Ghi Chú 01: Sự Phân Biệt Vùng Kiểm Soát Của Khắc Kỷ (Stoic Dichotomy of Control)

Triết lý Epictetus: Vạn vật trên đời chia làm 2 loại: Những điều phụ thuộc vào ta (Ý nghĩ, hành vi, phản ứng, đạo đức) và Những điều không phụ thuộc vào ta (Thời tiết, thị trường, ý kiến người khác, bệnh tật, cái chết).

Trí tuệ: Dành 100% năng lượng cho những điều ta kiểm soát được; đón nhận thanh thản những điều ngoài tầm kiểm soát.

Ứng dụng: Khi gặp biến cố bất ngờ, tự hỏi ngay: "Tôi có thể kiểm soát điều này không?". Nếu không, hãy buông bỏ sự lo lắng vô ích.

🔗 https://taichinow.github.io/articles/07_psychology_philosophy_10_notes

📌 10 Ghi Chú Cốt Tủy: Hành Trình Thức Tỉnh & Khoa Học Tâm Linh Toàn Diện

Ghi Chú 01: Nhận Thức Tỉnh Thức (Pure Awareness & The Witness)

Bản chất: Bạn không phải là suy nghĩ của bạn, bạn không phải là cảm xúc của bạn; bạn là "Người Quan Sát" (The Observer) nhận biết những suy nghĩ và cảm xúc đó sinh khởi và tan biến.

Tác dụng: Giải phóng hoàn toàn bản thân khỏi sự đồng hóa với những cơn giận dữ, lo âu hay trầm cảm.

Ứng dụng: Khi có cảm xúc tiêu cực khởi lên, thầm nhủ: "Tôi đang quan sát cảm xúc này xuất hiện, nhưng tôi không phải là nó".

Ghi Chú 02: Sức Mạnh Của Hiện Tại (The Power of Now - Eckhart Tolle)

📌 The 24-Form at a Glance

Why the 24-Form Exists

The 24-Form (Nhị Thập Tứ Thức) was standardised by the Chinese Sports Commission in 1956, distilled from the Yang tradition into a complete beginner's curriculum. It is not the deepest practice in the art. It is the easiest entry point that still carries the full structure of Tai Chi: 8 Gates, 5 Steps, soft-hard alternation, breath coordination, weight transfer. It completes in 5–8 minutes and can be practised almost anywhere.

items.message:
📌 Yin-Yang and the Dance of Opposites

The Dance

Yin-Yang is not a static symbol. It is a dance: every Yang contains a seed of Yin, every Yin contains a seed of Yang, and the boundary between them is curved — not a clean line. In Tai Chi, every movement embodies this dance: open and close, advance and retreat, hard and soft, full and empty. The art teaches you to see the dance, then to be the dance.

Where You See It in the Form

items.message:
📌 An (Án / 按) — Push

The Big Idea

An (Án / 按) is the finishing stroke. If Peng is the sphere, Ji is the compression, An is the resolution. The energy has been redirected back toward the opponent and now travels downward — through them, into the ground. An is the difference between a push that moves someone and a push that roots them.

An is issued from a settled center. The kua (inguinal fold) drops, the tailbone sinks, the breath sinks. The hands appear to follow, but in fact the center has already moved — the hands just complete the picture.

Drills

items.message:
📌 Eight Trigrams (Bát Quái / 八卦) — Mapping Internal Directions

The Big Idea

Bát Quái (八卦 / Eight Trigrams) in Tai Chi map the body's internal compass: the directions of energy flow. Each trigram corresponds to a body region and movement quality: Khảm = back/descending, Lý = front/ascending, Cấm = internal/restraining, Đoàn = lateral/releasing, Chấn = upspringing, Khôn = downcending. The advanced student reads their body's Bát Quái map — when energy flows to the back (Khảm), the body sinks; when to the front (Lý), it rises. Recognizing which trigram is active tells you what adjustment the body needs.

items.message:
📌 Opening Eight Directions (Bát Hướng) — Structure Before Reach

The Big Idea

Bát Hướng (Opening Eight Directions) is a stance and movement pattern that establishes the body's axes — forward/back, left/right, up/down — all anchored simultaneously. You are a cross: arms outstretched, legs in horse stance, feet rooting into earth and sky.

The movement principle: each direction is a door. When you push forward, the back door opens. When you pull back, the front door opens. The 50+ body needs this spatial awareness to compensate for the narrowed peripheral vision that aging brings. Bát Hướng is literally "opening" to the world again.

Drills

items.message:
📌 The 3-Anchor Check, 3-Question Diagnostic, One-Word Cues

The 3-Anchor Check

The three anchors are weight, breath, and intention. Run them every few minutes during practice. Where is my weight right now — forward, back, left, right? Where is my breath — high in the chest, low in the dantian, somewhere in between? Where is my intention — on the movement in front of me, on the next movement, wandering in thought?

The check is a 5-second audit. It does not interrupt the practice — it deepens it. The anchors become internal GPS coordinates the body uses to organise itself.

The 3-Question Diagnostic

items.message:
📌 The 30-Minute Daily Form

What the 30-Minute Form Looks Like

A complete Tai Chi practice in 30 minutes is broken into three blocks of ten minutes: warm-up, form, cool-down. The warm-up is Jing Gong (quiet standing) plus a few release movements. The form is one or two repetitions of your current form. The cool-down is hands-on self-massage along the meridians, ending with three still breaths.

The Three Anchors Within the Half-Hour

items.message:
📌 The 7 Deadly Sins of the 3.0 Student

The Seven Sins

Almost every common beginner mistake falls into one of seven categories. Each is a way of forcing what should be allowed:

Holding the breath — power surges in the shoulders and neck.

Leading with the arms — the body becomes a passenger.

Locking the knees — the lower joints stop transmitting force.

Puffing the chest — breath rises, the lower dantian empties.

Double-loading — weight shared by both feet, both hands. No waves, no structure.

Sinking the shoulders too far — not sōng but sui. The chest collapses.

🔗 https://taichinow.github.io/techniques/bay-sai-lam

items.message:
📌 Why Slow Is Fast

Tai Chi looks slow from the outside. Inside, it is densely packed: every micro-position is corrected, every joint angle is debated, every breath is placed. The 30-minute slow form packs more learning than a 10-minute fast form because the brain has time to absorb each layer. Slow is the speed at which skill compounds.

Speed is a downstream effect. When the structure is correct, when the breath is correct, when the rhythm is correct, speed emerges naturally. Trying to be fast when the foundation is shallow produces external movement without internal content.

Slow as Diagnostic

items.message:
📌 Suspended & Heavy (Chanh / 穿) — Coordinating Lightness and Weight

The Big Idea

Chanh Treo Nặng (Suspended & Heavy) describes the coordination between two seemingly opposite qualities: Chanh (穿) — the sensation of threading or piercing, where energy passes through the limbs like a needle through silk; Dun (顿) — the sudden stop, where all energy gathers and drops like a stone.

Chanh is light, threading, continuous. Dun is heavy, gathering, sudden. The advanced skill is to weave them in a single movement: as the left hand threads out (Chanh), the right hand gathers in (Dun). The form alternates: thread, gather, thread, gather.

📌 Silk Reeling Energy (Chan Si Jin / 缠丝劲) — The Spiral of Integrated Power

The Big Idea

Chan Si Jin (缠丝劲 / Silk Reeling Energy) is the spiraling, coiling force that runs through the entire body. Unlike linear force (which travels in a straight line from A to B), spiral force wraps around the body's axis like a spring. Every joint contributes a rotation; every step adds a twist. The energy never travels directly — it always curves, always coils, always returns.

📌 The 50+ Body as Taichi's Perfect Instrument

Why the 50+ Body Is Perfect

The 50+ body is not a diminished 30-year-old body. It is a different instrument — one that Tai Chi was essentially designed for. The art's slow pace matches a metabolism that no longer tolerates explosive training. Its attention to breath supports the cardiovascular system as arteries stiffen. Its balance work prevents the falls that are the leading cause of injury death in older adults. Its weight-bearing slow movements maintain bone density better than moderate-impact exercise.

Đan Điền (丹田 / Dantian) is the energy center located 2-3 inches below the navel, roughly the size of a golf ball. It is not merely metaphorical — modern somatic practitioners identify it with the deep transverse abdominal muscles, the pelvic floor, and the diaphragm. These three muscle groups form a hydraulic unit: when they engage together, they create internal pressure that stabilizes the spine and powers the limbs.

items.message:
📌 Brush Knee (Diân / 剪) — The Universal Adjustment

The Big Idea

Brush Knee (Diên / 剪) is the most repeated movement in the 24-form — and the most done carelessly. At its core it is a coordination test: the waist rotates to bring the front hand across the body, the rear hand follows, and the step adjusts. All three parts must move together.

If the waist stops halfway, the front hand pulls too far and the shoulder collapses ("sheep shoulder"). If the step does not adjust, the hip binds. Brush Knee is the form's built-in diagnostic: do your parts still move as one?

Drills

🔗 https://taichinow.github.io/techniques/dien

items.message:
📌 Fixed Stability (Ding / 定) — Unshakeable Center

The Big Idea

Ding (定 / Fixed Stability) is the ability to remain completely unshakeable in the center while all movement occurs around you. Unlike 3.0 alignment (which requires active micro-adjustment), Ding is passive — a state of inherent balance where the center never deviates. Three components:

1. Central Pillar — the vertical line from heel through dantian to crown, unbroken regardless of limb movement. 2. Grounded Base — feet rooted so that impact travels straight down. 3. Quiet Center — the mind remains still while the body moves.

items.message:
📌 The Four Primary Energies (Pháp / 八) — Peng, Lu, Ji, An as Unified Skill

The Big Idea

The Four Primary Energies (Bát / 八) are the foundational forces of Tai Chi technique: Peng (Pháp / ward-off, upward), Lu (Lượ / rollback, inward), Ji (Tỳ / press, down-and-across), and An (Án / push, forward).

At the 4.0 level, these are no longer seen as four separate techniques but as a rotating tetrahedron: Peng feeds into Lu (what goes up must come down), Lu feeds into Ji (inward energy turns down), Ji feeds into An (gathered energy pushes forward), An feeds back into Peng (forward energy rises). The tetrahedron spins continuously.

items.message:
📌 Flowing Steps (Hoa Bước / 化步) — Neutral, Not Passive

The Big Idea

Hoa Bước (化步 / Flowing Step) is the step of redirection. Instead of meeting an opponent's push with resistance, you flow around it like water parting around a stone. The name "Hoa" means "to flow" or "to transform," not "to soften passively."

The technique: as force enters, you step offline — not backward (that is retreat), not forward (that is collision), but at an angle. The angle absorbs the force into the ground through your legs. This is why Hoa Bước is the antidote to San Shou’s direct engagement.

Drills

#ThaiCucQuyen #TaichiNow #SucKhoe

📌 Hua Jin (Hóa Tấn / 化勁) — Transforming Power Into Neutralization

The Big Idea

Hua Jin (化勁 / Transforming Power) is the skill of receiving incoming force and redirecting it so it dissipates rather than rebounds. Unlike Bao (containing), which absorbs and holds, Hua transforms and releases. The four Hua skills:

1. Dai Jin (Holding) — force is caught like silk worms. 2. Tiao Jin (Luring) — force is guided to a neutral point. 3. Tui Jin (Plowing) — force is redirected downward. 4. Tuo Jin (Lifting) — force is redirected upward. Together they form a continuous cycle of transformation.

items.message:
📌 Ji (Tỳ / 挤) — Press

The Big Idea

Ji (Tỳ / 挤) is whole-body expression. Where Peng is the sphere of readiness around you, Ji is what happens when that sphere is compressed and projected outward in a single line. Imagine holding the energy at your chest, then squeezing both forearms toward each other and forward — not with the arms, but with the whole structure behind the arms.

Ji issues from the back foot through the spine into the hands. The arms are the messengers; the hips and back are the engine. A common mistake is to press with the arms alone — this is a shoulder exercise, not Ji.

Drills

items.message:
📌 Emerging Step (Khai Bước / 開步) — Mechanics of the Expanding Stance

The Big Idea

Khai Bước (開步 / Emerging Step) is the technique of extending the step beyond its natural limit while maintaining full connection to the ground. Unlike a simple step forward (which can lose root as the foot passes over the ankle), Kai Bu keeps energy descending continuously. Three phases:

1. Preparation — weight shifts onto the ball of the standing foot. 2. Extension — the stepping leg extends forward, energy threading through the heel. 3. Landing — the foot lands with the heel touching first, then the whole sole, weight transferring smoothly.

items.message:
📌 Rowing the Chariot (Khai Gôn / 开功) — The First Real Alignment

The Big Idea

Khai Gôn (開功 / Rowing the Chariot) is the second movement of the form, the moment when your body first learns to coordinate front and back. The front hand pushes forward (palms down) while the rear hand pulls back (palms up). The spine lengthens; the waist turns; the step adjusts. This is the first full-body pattern students can actually feel.

Before Khai Gôn, most students move in fragments. After Khai Gôn, the body must decide: move as one, or never move at all in Tai Chi.

items.message:
📌 Merging Energy (Hòa Nhập / 合并) — Becoming One with the Push

The Big Idea

Hòa Nhập (合并 / Merging Energy) is the push-hands skill where your energy and your partner's energy become indistinguishable. Unlike 3.0 (where you feel a push coming and redirect it), Hòa Nhập means you can no longer tell which energy is yours and which is theirs — you have merged into a single energy field.

This happens when structure is so completely unified that there is no boundary between self and other. The telltale sign: after a session, you may not identify what push you initiated and what your partner initiated. You moved as one organism.

items.message:
📌 Mushin (Vô Tâm / 無心) — Mind of No-Mind

What Mushin Is

Mushin (無心) is the Japanese term that survived into the martial arts vocabulary; the original Chinese is wú xīn (無心). It means "no mind" — not no thought, but no gripping on thought. The mind is clear, responsive, and unattached to any single plan.

The everyday mind plans: I will do this, then this, then this. The mushin mind observes: What is here? What wants to happen? When a situation shifts, the planning mind scrambles to keep up; the mushin mind is already there.

Why It Matters for Tai Chi

items.message:
📌 The 5-Minute Standing Practice

Five Minutes That Reshape the Body

Five minutes of Ôm Thụ (Hugging the Tree) each day, done consistently over weeks, is more transformative than one 60-minute weekly class. The body learns what standing feels like when there is no agenda, no sequence, no movement to hide behind. Just the body and the breath.

By week 4, students report — without being told to look — that their normal standing posture has improved. By week 8, the slow form has visibly deepened. By week 12, chronic tightness in the shoulders or lower back often releases.

The 30-Day Cure

items.message:
📌 Counter-Step (Nghịch Bước / 逆步) — Adhere, Stick, and Yield

The Big Idea

Nghịch Bước (Counter-Step / 逆步) is the step of yielding. When an opponent pushes forward, instead of meeting their force, you step backward and offline at a 45-degree angle. This does two things: (1) it puts your body outside the line of their force, and (2) it positions your rear foot to drive the counter-redirect.

Crucial: Nghịch Bước is not retreat. A retreat steps straight back, leaving the force to dissipate harmlessly. A counter-step steps offline while maintaining root pressure — you are still grounded, still ready to return the redirection.

📌 The Tension Paradox — Why Strong Muscles Make Weak Taichi

The Paradox

The most common shock in any Tai Chi class is when a 50-year-old office worker — who cannot lift their bodyweight and has not exercised in 20 years — produces a sharper fajin than a fit 30-year-old gym-goer. The reason is not magic. It is that Tai Chi uses a different muscular pathway: fascia, not muscle.

📌 Reverse Breathing (Nghịch Thở / 逆呼吸)

What Reverse Breathing Is

In normal breathing, the abdomen expands on inhale, contracts on exhale. In Nghịch Thở (reverse breathing), the abdomen contracts on inhale and expands on exhale. This reversal increases the negative pressure in the lower abdomen during inhalation and pumps the lower dantian on exhalation.

items.message:
📌 Hugging the Tree (Ôm Thụ / 抱树)

The Posture

Hugging the Tree (Ôm Thụ / 抱树) is the foundational Zhan Zhuang (Trụ Thế / standing meditation) posture. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent, arms held in front of the chest as if embracing a large tree — rounded, suspended, alive.

It looks like nothing is happening. Everything is happening. The body is learning to stand with structure, to breathe into the lower dantian, to release tension from the nine checkpoints of sōng, and to remain patient.

The 5-Minute Practice That Changes Everything

The \'pot\' refers to the dantian — the belly is the vessel, and the arms are the lid that seals it. When done correctly, this creates a pressurized chamber: the dantian is compressed, the energy circulates, and power can issue in any direction.

📌 Peng (Phòng / 掤) — Ward Off

The Big Idea

Peng (Phòng / 掤) is the foundational energy of Tai Chi Chuan. It is not a block or a ward-off in the karate sense. It is a sphere of organized readiness around the body — imagine an invisible ball of pressurized air that surrounds you. When something presses in, the sphere pushes back, not with muscular force, but with the integrated structure of bones, joints, and connective tissue.

📌 The 5-Minute Reset Practice for Busy Days

The Five-Minute Reset

On days when the schedule has eaten the practice, when travel has interrupted everything, when the body is sore from a tennis match or a long meeting, you can still recover five minutes. The sequence:

1. 60 seconds dantian breath, seated or standing.

2. 60 seconds spinal roll-down: chin to chest, vertebra by vertebra.

3. 60 seconds shoulder circles: both directions, slow.

4. 60 seconds ankle rotations: seated, both feet, both directions.

5. 60 seconds Ôm Thụ lite: standing, three breaths.

items.title: The 5-Minute Reset Practice for Busy Days
items.excerpt:
The Five-Minute Reset

On days when the schedule has eaten the practice, when travel has interrupted everything, when the body is sore from a tennis match or a long meeting, you can still recover five minutes. The sequence:

1. 60 seconds dantian breath, seated or standing.

2. 60 seconds spinal roll-down: chin to chest, vertebra by vertebra.

3. 60 seconds shoulder circles: both directions, slow.

4. 60 seconds ankle rotations: seated, both feet, both directions.

5. 60 seconds Ôm Thụ lite: standing, three breaths.

items.message:
📌 Root & Suspend (Neo & Treo) — The Dual Anchors of Structural Integrity

The Big Idea

Neo & Treo (Root & Suspend) are the two poles of structural integrity. Neo (Root) means the body connects downward to the earth — legs drive energy into the ground, the ground pushes back. Treo (Suspend) means the body connects upward to the sky — the head floats, the spine lengthens, the crown lifts without effort. Both must be simultaneous.

Drills

String Test — Stand in Wuji. Imagine a string pulls your crown upward, and a string pushes your tailbone downward. Neither should be taut. Have a partner push on your shoulder: if correct, you will not move at all.

items.message:
📌 San Shou (Free-Hand Push Hands) — Contact Without Armor

The Big Idea

San Shou (Tự Thủ) — free-hand push hands — is the first place you test your structure outside of a mirror. One partner offers a light push; the other receives and returns. Unlike external push hands (where people trade force), San Shou operates on neutral meeting: the contact point does not lock; it adheres, sticks, and connects.

The goal is not to win a shove. The goal is to feel the opponent's center — their balance, intention, next micro-movement — before they commit. This is why San Shou is called "listening hands."

Drills

items.message:
📌 Guardian Posture (Thủ Bát Bảo) — Protecting Your Center

The Big Idea

Thủ Bát Bảo (Guardian Posture) appears in the 24-form as "Hug the Sparrow" and in the 108-form at several points. The imagery: you are guarding a treasure (a bowl of rice, a child, a secret). Your arms form a protective circle around your center; your legs root wide to resist any direction of force.

The technique principle: the center never moves. The arms and legs respond — they do not lead. When a partner pushes your left arm, your right leg pushes back into the ground. The force does not meet at the contact; it is resolved in the earth through the opposite leg.

Drills

📌 Advanced Silk-Reeling Drills (Chan Si Jin Nâng Cao)

The Big Idea

Chan Si Jin Nâng Cao (Advanced Silk-Reeling) builds on basic spiral by introducing multi-plane rotation. Where beginner silk-reeling spirals through the vertical axis, advanced silk-reeling spirals through all three planes: frontal, sagittal, and transverse simultaneously. The body becomes a triple-helix — like DNA, with energy tracing a 3D corkscrew through every joint.

items.message:
📌 The Body Schema — Weight, Ground, Alignment

Three Maps You Always Carry

Every Tai Chi movement is the body's answer to three questions: where is my weight? (forward/back/left/right); where is the ground? (which points of the foot are pressing, which are light); where is my alignment? (is the spine vertical, is the breath unobstructed). Most beginners carry only one of these maps at a time. Experienced practitioners carry all three simultaneously, and the body answers them without thinking.

Drill: The Three Maps in One Minute

items.message:
📌 Letting Go of Energy (Thiu / 松) — Unwinding Force

The Big Idea

Thiu (松 / Letting Go of Energy) is the active release of stored energy, distinct from passive relaxation. Where relaxation is letting go unconsciously, Thiu is a deliberate decision to release specific energy from a specific location.

The three types of Thiu: (1) Thiu thần (Relax the Mind) — releasing mental tension. (2) Thiu khí (Relax the Energy) — releasing built-up qi from a specific channel. (3) Thiu xương (Relax the Bone) — releasing deep structural tension.

items.message:
📌 Collapse (Sụp / 塌) — The Deliberate Surrender Into Structure

The Big Idea

Sụp (塌 / Collapse) is the counterpoint to Tăng (to rise). While the 3.0 student learns to open, the 4.0 student learns to collapse — deliberately, structurally, and safely. Sụp is not about falling apart; it is about failing into structure. Three types: (1) Sụp xuống — dantian softens and sinks. (2) Sụp vào — chest releases and ribs draw in. (3) Sụp lùi — spine releases extension and curves naturally.

Drills

items.message:
📌 Spontaneous Movement (Tự Sinh / 自生) — When Form Dissolves

The Big Idea

Tự Sinh (自生 / Spontaneous Movement) is the stage where the form dissolves and movement arises on its own — not from muscle memory, not from conscious direction, but from the body's intrinsic intelligence. Movements may look like miniature forms, or nothing like the form at all — fluid, asymmetrical, unpredictable.

Three signs you are in Tự Sinh: (1) No memory of deciding — movement happened and you were the witness. (2) No effort to sustain — it arose and passed without volition. (3) Embodied knowing — afterward you understand something about your structure.

Drills

items.message:
📌 Sōng (松) — Nine Points of Relaxation

What Sōng Really Means

Sōng (松) is often translated as "relaxation," but it does not mean "loose" or "floppy." It means a specific kind of relaxation: release of unnecessary muscular tension while maintaining structural integrity. The bones hold the shape; the muscles do not grip. The joints are open; the tendons are slack; the body is ready to move in any direction at any moment.

The opposite is sūi (塌) — collapse. Sung keeps the structure upright; sūi lets it fall. The difference is between relaxed muscles and abandoned posture.

The Nine Points of Relaxation

📌 The Three Treasures (Tam Bảo) — Jing, Qi, Shen

The Three Treasures

The Tam Bảo (Three Treasures) are the three layers of the human system that Tai Chi refines in order: Jing (精) essence, stored in the kidneys; Qi (氣) life energy, cultivated at the Dantian; Shen (神) spirit, expressed through the eyes and the will. The practice refines Jing into Qi, and Qi into Shen. This is not a metaphor — it is a description of what actually happens to the body and mind with daily practice.

items.message:
📌 Substantial & Insubstantial Stepping (Tấn Hư Tấn Thực)

Stepping as Hư/Thực in Motion

Every step in the form is a small story of substantial and insubstantial. The back foot leaves the ground only when it has nothing more to do (it has become empty). The forward foot settles into the ground only when it is ready to bear weight (it has become full). The middle of the step — when the entire body's weight is balanced between the two feet — is the riskiest moment. The skill is to pass through it quickly.

Three Common Errors

Twenty minutes at home, with no teacher, no equipment, no music, can be one of the most reliable daily practices in Tai Chi. The structure is simple: 5 minutes Ôm Thụ, 10 minutes slow form, 5 minutes standing meditation and breath.

That is the entire practice. The room can be small. The floor can be a carpet. The shoes can be socks.

Substitutions When You Cannot Do the Form

items.message:
📌 Grasp Sparrow's Tail Summary — The Four Gates at a Glance

The Big Idea

Lãm Tưọc Vỹ (Grasp Sparrow's Tail) is the signature sequence of Yang-style Tai Chi: Peng → Lu → Ji → An → Turn → Repulse. It combines all four primary energies in one flowing phrase. You will practice it 4 times in the 24-form — twice on each side.

The sequence teaches four things simultaneously: (1) the four energies flow as one wave, (2) each energy has its own precise hand shape, (3) the waist turns to carry the next movement, (4) the step adjusts to ground each transition. Mastery is not memorizing the shape — it is feeling the wave.

Drills

items.message:
📌 Dan Tian Breathing — Lower Abdomen, Lower Dantian

What Dan Tian Breathing Is

Dan Tian breathing means breathing into the lower abdomen — not the chest, not the shoulders, but the area roughly 3 cm below the navel, deep inside the pelvis. On inhale the belly expands outward; on exhale it draws back in. Most adults have lost this pattern (stress, posture, sedentary habits). Children breathe this way naturally. Tai Chi restores it.

📌 Listening Energy (Ting Jin / 听劲) — The Skill of Feeling Before Moving

The Big Idea

Ting Jin (听劲 / Listening Energy) is the highest skill in push hands — the ability to sense an opponent's state of balance, intention, and next movement through touch alone. Ting Jin does not predict; it perceives in real-time. When developed, it allows you to feel the opponent’s center of gravity shift before they are consciously aware of it themselves.

items.message:
📌 Lifting the Paten (Tô Hô) — Supporting the Unsupported

The Big Idea

Tô Hô (Lifting the Paten) appears in the 24-form as Part the Wild Horse's Mane and in the 42-form as Lift the Paten. The imagery is borrowed from Buddhist temple life: the paten (the plate that holds the offering) is lifted with two hands, slowly, with the whole body.

In Tai Chi, Tô Hô is a full-body integration movement. The front hand does not grab; it supports. The waist rotates to lift; the legs root to stabilize. The arms act as extensions of the spine, not independent movers. This is why Tô Hô is so revealing — it shows whether your arm is connected to your dantian.

🔗 https://taichinow.github.io/techniques/tu-hu

items.message:
📌 Empty Void (Thê / 空) — The Meaning Beyond Form

The Big Idea

Tu Không (Thê / 空 / Empty Void) is the understanding that the form exists only as a doorway, not as a destination. When you can perform the form correctly but feel no attachment to its accuracy, you have entered the void. Tu means 'to void, empty.' Yi means 'meaning, significance.'

Tu Yi is the moment in practice when the form dissolves and you are no longer performing — you are simply moving according to the body's intrinsic intelligence. This is not nihilistic emptiness; it is the clearing of space for what is needed in the moment.

🔗 https://taichinow.github.io/techniques/tu-yi

items.message:
📌 The Wu Wei Stance (Vô Vi) and the Standing Post (Trụ Thế)

The Stance and the Post

The Wu Wei (Vô Vi) Stance is the basic standing position: feet shoulder-width apart, knees soft, tailbone dropping, crown suspended. The Standing Post (Trụ Thế / Zhan Zhuang) is what you do in that stance: stand, breathe, wait. Both look identical from the outside. The first is a position; the second is a practice.

The Wu Wei stance without Zhan Zhuang is just posture. Zhan Zhuang without the Wu Wei stance is just standing. Together they form the seed of the entire art. Five minutes a day for a month produces visible changes in any beginner.

🔗 https://taichinow.github.io/techniques/vo-vi-tru-the

📌 Wu Wei (Vô Vi / 无为) — The Art of Non-Action in Motion

The Big Idea

Vô Vi (無為 / Wu Wei) is the most misunderstood and most powerful concept in Tai Chi — for good reason. Literally "non-action" or "non-doing," Vô Vi does NOT mean doing nothing. It means acting without forcing. The action arises naturally from the situation; no extra effort or intention is added.

items.message:
📌 Five Elements (Ngũ Hành / 五行) — The Cycles of Energetic Transformation

The Big Idea

Ngũ Hành (五行 / Five Elements) in Tai Chi is an energetic map of how forces transform and interact: the Generating Cycle (Wood→Fire→Earth→Metal→Water→Wood) and the Overcoming Cycle (Wood→Earth→Water→Fire→Metal→Wood). In movement, each direction has an elemental quality: forward is Fire (expanding), backward is Water (descending), left is Wood (growing), right is Metal (cutting), center is Earth (stabilizing). When your form flows correctly through Ngũ Hành, energy transforms smoothly without stagnation.

items.message:
📌 Twist Step (Quay / 轉) — Redirecting Power Through the Waist

The Big Idea

Twist Step (Quay / 轉 bước) is where Waist (Dẫn Bất Đối) meets Step (Bước Thật). The feet plant firmly to anchor; the waist rotates to redirect; the step carries the redirect. Unlike a pivot (which rotates around a fixed axis), twist step is a traveling rotation: the axis moves through the body as the center shifts.

The power vector shifts from vertical (root) to horizontal (redirect). The 50+ body often does this backwards — twisting from the shoulders or knees. The correct path: root through the feet, rotate from the dantian, land the step with the center forward.

Drills

items.message:
📌 Xū & Shí (Hư & Thực / 虚实) — Empty and Solid

The Core Operating Principle

Hư (虚 / empty) and Thực (实 / full or solid) are the operating principle behind every movement. One leg is full, the other is empty. One hand is full, the other is empty. One direction is full, the other is empty. At every moment the body is moving between full and empty like waves.

A common error is to be double full — weight on both feet, tension in both hands. Another is double empty — weight floating, structure unsupported. Single full, single empty. Always.

Why This Matters at 50+

items.message:
📌 Yi → Qi → Body (Ý → Khí → Thân)

The Transmission Sequence

The classical sequence is Ý dẫn Khí, Khí dẫn Thân (意 → 氣 → 身): Yì (Intention) leads Qì (Energy), Qì leads the Body. This is the operating system of the internal arts. It is not a metaphor — it is the order in which things must move if they are to be guided rather than forced.

If the body leads, you have external movement without internal content — gymnastics. If the breath leads, you have energy movement without destination — qigong exercise. If intention leads, the body follows breath follows intention — this is internal martial art.

The Three Drills

📌 Yin-Yang Integration (Âm Dương Hòa Nhất) — The Neutral Zone

The Big Idea

Âm Dương Hòa Nhất (Yin-Yang Integration) is where the practitioner transcends effort to distinguish between hard and soft, full and empty, up and down. These distinctions dissolve into a single flowing motion that is simultaneously both. The integration works through the neutral zone: a small range where the body transitions between Yin and Yang without falling into either extreme.

items.message:
📌 The Yin-Yang Energy Loop (Âm Dương Tuần Hoàn) — Circular Power

The Big Idea

The Yin-Yang Energy Loop (Vòng Tròn Âm Dương) is the circular flow of energy through the body's front and back pathways. The front channel (Ren / Nhân) carries Yin energy (nourishing, descending); the back channel (Du / Đố) carries Yang energy (transforming, ascending). These two channels form an endless loop: energy descends the front, transforms at the dantian, and ascends the back, only to descend again.

items.message:
📌 Central Equilibrium (Trung Nghị / 中定) — The Middle Way of Balance

The Big Idea

Trung Nghị (中定 / Central Equilibrium) is the Tai Chi skill of occupying exactly the center of gravity — never falling to the left, never falling to the right, never advancing or retreating. The Chinese classic describes this as "being like a great weight balanced on nothing." The body has a single point of balance, and every movement must return to that center.

🔗 https://taichinow.github.io/techniques/zhong-ning

The Big Idea

Trăng (Trượt / Zhuó Tiān / Circling the Moon) is the hidden spiral that connects the left and right sides of the body through the dantian. While Grasp Sparrow's Tail appears to be four separate movements (Ward Off, Roll Back, Press, Push), the advanced view sees them as one continuous spiral: the energy enters through the left hand (Ward Off), crosses the dantian, emerges through the right hand (Push), and the other three are transition phases.

📌 10 Ghi Chú Cốt Tủy: Thái Cực Quyền, Khí Công & Cơ Sinh Học Cân Mạc (Taichi-ChiGong)

Ghi Chú 01: Khái Niệm "Tùng" (Sung) — Khử Co Cứng Đối Kháng

Bản chất: Tùng không phải là buông xuôi nhẽo cơ mà là trạng thái giải tỏa co thắt cơ vân đối kháng (antagonist muscle inhibition), cho phép năng lượng truyền tải tự do qua các khớp.

Cơ chế cân mạc: Giảm ma sát nội mô, tăng dịch bôi trơn hyaluronic acid giữa các lớp màng cân mạc (fascial glide).

Ứng dụng thực hành: Khi đứng Trạm Trang, liên tục rà soát quét từ đỉnh đầu xuống bàn chân để "tháo van" mọi điểm gồng cứng vô thức.

Ghi Chú 02: Hư Linh Đỉnh Kình & Trục Cột Sống Treo

🔗 https://taichinow.github.io/vi/articles/01_taichi_qigong_10_notes

📌 10 Ghi Chú Cốt Tủy: Y Học Cổ Truyền (TCM), Kinh Lạc & Năng Lượng Tự Chữa Lành

Ghi Chú 01: Đồng Hồ Sinh Học 12 Kinh Lạc (TCM Circadian Organ Clock)

Bản chất: Mỗi tạng phủ có 2 giờ hoạt động với năng lượng khí huyết cao nhất trong ngày.

Quy luật: Phế (3-5h), Đại Trường (5-7h), Vị (7-9h), Tỳ (9-11h), Tâm (11-13h), Tiểu Trường (13-15h), Bàng Quang (15-17h), Thận (17-19h), Tâm Bào (19-21h), Tam Tiêu (21-23h), Đởm (23-1h), Can (1-3h).

Ứng dụng: Không ăn đêm sau 20h để tránh cản trở Can-Đởm giải độc và phục hồi tủy.

Ghi Chú 02: Trục Thận Thủy - Tâm Hỏa (Thủy Hỏa Ký Tế)

Bản chất: Thận thủy cần bốc lên làm mát Tâm hỏa; Tâm hỏa cần giáng xuống sưởi ấm Thận thủy.

📌 10 Ghi Chú Cốt Tủy: Tuổi 52 — Hành Trình Tu Tập Nội Tại & Trí Tuệ Sống

Ghi Chú 01: Quy Luật "Ngũ Thập Tri Thiên Mệnh"

Ý nghĩa cốt lõi: Tuổi 50 không phải là sự già nua, mà là điểm khởi đầu của trí tuệ chín muồi. Biết rõ giới hạn của bản thân và hiểu quy luật của vũ trụ để sống thuận tự nhiên.

Tâm thế sống: Chuyển từ "chinh phục thế giới bên ngoài" sang "làm chủ thế giới nội tâm".

Ứng dụng: Buông bỏ nhu cầu chứng tỏ bản thân với xã hội, chỉ giữ lại những kết nối chân thành.

Ghi Chú 02: Tái Cấu Trúc Trục Cơ Thể Sau Tuổi 50

Thực trạng: Các đĩa đệm cột sống mất nước, mật độ xương giảm, các khớp gối và háng dễ thoái hóa nếu vận động sai trục.

🔗 https://taichinow.github.io/vi/articles/03_tuoi_52_tu_tap_noi_tai_10_notes

#ThaiCucQuyen #TaichiNow #SucKhoe

— Phạm Đức Hải

📌 10 Ghi Chú Cốt Tủy: Tự Lực & Trí Tuệ Thực Hành Đời Sống (Self-Help & Practical Wisdom)

Ghi Chú 01: Sức Mạnh Của Những Thói Quen Nguyên Tử (Atomic Habits)

Quy luật tích lũy: Tiến bộ 1% mỗi ngày tương đương với việc bạn sẽ giỏi hơn gấp 37 lần sau một năm.

Công thức 4 bước: Gợi ý (Cue) ──► Khao khát (Craving) ──► Phản hồi (Response) ──► Phần thưởng (Reward).

Ứng dụng: Ghép thói quen mới vào sau một thói quen cũ đã có sẵn (Habit Stacking).

📌 10 Ghi Chú Cốt Tủy: Huấn Luyện & Luyện Tập Có Chủ Đích (Coaching & Deliberate Practice)

Ghi Chú 01: Sự Khác Biệt Giữa Luyện Tập Thường (Naive Practice) & Có Chủ Đích (Deliberate Practice)

Luyện tập thường: Lặp đi lặp lại một hành động quen thuộc một cách vô thức, không có phản hồi và không có thử thách.

Luyện tập có chủ đích (Anders Ericsson): Mục tiêu cụ thể, tập trung 100%, vượt ra ngoài vùng thoải mái, có phản hồi tức thì và hiệu chỉnh liên tục.

Ứng dụng: Mỗi buổi tập Thái Cực hay kỹ năng đều phải có 1 mục tiêu kỹ thuật cụ thể cần cải thiện (ví dụ: chỉ tập trung mở khớp háng Kua trong 30 phút).

items.message:
📌 10 Ghi Chú Cốt Tủy: Tâm Lý Học Hành Vi & Triết Học Đời Sống (Psychology & Philosophy)

Ghi Chú 01: Sự Phân Biệt Vùng Kiểm Soát Của Khắc Kỷ (Stoic Dichotomy of Control)

Triết lý Epictetus: Vạn vật trên đời chia làm 2 loại: Những điều phụ thuộc vào ta (Ý nghĩ, hành vi, phản ứng, đạo đức) và Những điều không phụ thuộc vào ta (Thời tiết, thị trường, ý kiến người khác, bệnh tật, cái chết).

Trí tuệ: Dành 100% năng lượng cho những điều ta kiểm soát được; đón nhận thanh thản những điều ngoài tầm kiểm soát.

Ứng dụng: Khi gặp biến cố bất ngờ, tự hỏi ngay: "Tôi có thể kiểm soát điều này không?". Nếu không, hãy buông bỏ sự lo lắng vô ích.

🔗 https://taichinow.github.io/vi/articles/07_psychology_philosophy_10_notes

📌 10 Ghi Chú Cốt Tủy: Hành Trình Thức Tỉnh & Khoa Học Tâm Linh Toàn Diện

Ghi Chú 01: Nhận Thức Tỉnh Thức (Pure Awareness & The Witness)

Bản chất: Bạn không phải là suy nghĩ của bạn, bạn không phải là cảm xúc của bạn; bạn là "Người Quan Sát" (The Observer) nhận biết những suy nghĩ và cảm xúc đó sinh khởi và tan biến.

Tác dụng: Giải phóng hoàn toàn bản thân khỏi sự đồng hóa với những cơn giận dữ, lo âu hay trầm cảm.

Ứng dụng: Khi có cảm xúc tiêu cực khởi lên, thầm nhủ: "Tôi đang quan sát cảm xúc này xuất hiện, nhưng tôi không phải là nó".

Ghi Chú 02: Sức Mạnh Của Hiện Tại (The Power of Now - Eckhart Tolle)

Khi áp dụng vào tài chính và cuộc sống, Essentialism là chiếc la bàn giúp bảo toàn năng lượng, giải phóng tâm trí và tạo ra sự tự do tài chính đích thực.

📌 Taichi Practice Cheat Sheet | Tờ Gian Lận Tập Thái Cực

Print this. Fold it. Keep it in your tennis bag. / In ra. Gấp lại. Để trong túi tennis.

Daily 5-Minute Foundation | Nền Tảng 5 Phút Mỗi Ngày

🇺🇸 English

🇻🇳 Tiếng Việt

Time

1

Zhan Zhuang — stand like a tree: feet shoulder-width, knees soft, spine tall, hands rounded at belly.

Trạp Trang — đứng như cây: hai chân rộng vai, gối mềm, lưng thẳng, hai tay ôm tròn trước bụng.

Gần đây, người ta nói nhiều về "thuận theo tự nhiên". Có người bảo hãy bỏ phố về rừng, sống chan hòa với mây núi. Có người khuyên ăn thực vật, sống tối giản, buông bỏ mọi tham cầu. Lại có những khóa học "sống chậm" mọc lên như nấm, hứa hẹn chữa lành mọi tổn thương chỉ bằng cách... thả mình theo dòng đời.

items.message:
📌 Thuận theo tự nhiên

THUẬN THEO TỰ NHIÊN VÀ Ý KHÍ HỢP NHẤT

Một góc nhìn từ triết học Lão Trang, Y học cổ truyền và khoa học sinh lý

Gần đây, người ta nói nhiều về "thuận theo tự nhiên". Có người bảo hãy bỏ phố về rừng, sống chan hòa với mây núi. Có người khuyên ăn thực vật, sống tối giản, buông bỏ mọi tham cầu. Lại có những khóa học "sống chậm" mọc lên như nấm, hứa hẹn chữa lành mọi tổn thương chỉ bằng cách... thả mình theo dòng đời.

Nhưng liệu đó có thực sự là thuận theo tự nhiên?
